title: Building a Lao Language LLM with Gemma 4: A Complete Guide
excerpt: How I fine-tuned Google's Gemma 4 E4B model to understand and generate Lao text — covering vocab surgery, continual pre-training, and supervised fine-tuning from scratch.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Lao is a language that the AI world has largely forgotten. With fewer than 100 million speakers and a shortage of digitized text, building a language model from scratch just didn't make sense — too expensive, too inefficient, and frankly, not the smartest use of resources.
So I took a different approach. Instead of starting from zero, I took Google's Gemma 4 E4B — a capable 4-billion-parameter multimodal model — and essentially taught it Lao. Step by step, I adapted a model built for dominant, western-centric languages into something that could actually read, understand, and write fluent Lao.

sections.title: Step 1 — Collect Lao Language Data
sections.body:
After I fetched all Lao text sources, I followed this exact next pipeline to produce a usable Lao tokenizer model.

Step 1) Normalize every fetched Lao file (not only one file) to ensure consistent Unicode, filtering, and dedup quality.
```python
from pathlib import Path
from subprocess import run

for src in Path("data/raw").glob("*.txt"):
    dst = Path("data/processed") / f"{src.stem}_clean.txt"
    run([
        "python", "scripts/normalize_lao.py",
        str(src), str(dst), "--filter-lao", "0.30", "--dedup"
    ], check=True)
```

Step 2) Merge all normalized files into one training corpus for tokenizer training.
```python
from pathlib import Path

parts = [p.read_text(encoding="utf-8") for p in Path("data/processed").glob("*_clean.txt")]
Path("data/processed/all_lao_clean.txt").write_text("\n".join(parts), encoding="utf-8")
```

Step 3) Train the Lao tokenizer model from the merged normalized corpus.
```python
from subprocess import run

run([
    "python", "models/tokenizer/train_tokenizer.py",
    "--corpus", "data/processed/all_lao_clean.txt",
    "--output-dir", "models/tokenizer/lao_tokenizer_v1"
], check=True)
```

Step 4) Test tokenizer quality and loading behavior before using it in downstream training.
```python
from subprocess import run

run([
    "python", "models/tokenizer/train_tokenizer.py",
    "--test-only",
    "--model-dir", "models/tokenizer/lao_tokenizer_v1/hf_tokenizer"
], check=True)
```

Result: this flow gives a reproducible Lao tokenizer model trained from all fetched and normalized Lao data.

Credit: data collection inspiration and source references from GitHub user therngbtg (https://github.com/therngbtg), LinkedIn (https://www.linkedin.com/in/bountherng-phetlasy-489a3316b/).

sections.title: Step 2 — Tokenizer Audit and Vocab Surgery
sections.body:
Step 2 is the full tokenizer surgery workflow after Step 1 data collection and normalization. First, I extract Lao tokens that exist in my tokenizer but do not exist in Gemma 4. Then I clean noisy tokens, add clean Lao tokens to Gemma, validate before/after tokenization quality, and save a new surgery-ready base model.

Step 2.1) Extract missing Lao tokens from Gemma.
```python
import json
import sentencepiece as spm
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

gemma_tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/gemma-4-E4B", trust_remote_code=True)
lao_sp = spm.SentencePieceProcessor(model_file="lao_spm.model")

def is_lao(text):
    return any("\u0e80" <= ch <= "\u0eff" for ch in text)

lao_vocab = [lao_sp.id_to_piece(i) for i in range(lao_sp.get_piece_size())]
lao_vocab = [t for t in lao_vocab if is_lao(t)]
new_tokens = sorted([t for t in lao_vocab if t not in gemma_tok.get_vocab()])

json.dump({"tokens": new_tokens, "gemma_original_vocab": len(gemma_tok)}, open("lao_missing_tokens.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
```

Step 2.2) Clean missing tokens (remove noisy tokens before surgery).
```python
import json

data = json.load(open("lao_missing_tokens.json", "r", encoding="utf-8"))
raw_tokens = data["tokens"]

def is_clean_lao_token(token):
    t = token.replace("▁", "")
    if not t or len(t) > 30:
        return False
    if t[0] in '()[]{}.,;:!?"\'/\\@#$%^&*+=<>~`' or t[-1] in '()[]{}.,;:!?"\'/\\@#$%^&*+=<>~`':
        return False
    if any(c in t for c in "()[]{}"):
        return False
    lao_chars = sum(1 for c in t if 0x0E80 <= ord(c) <= 0x0EFF)
    return lao_chars > 0 and lao_chars / len(t) >= 0.5

clean_tokens = sorted([t for t in raw_tokens if is_clean_lao_token(t)])
json.dump({"tokens": clean_tokens, "gemma_original_vocab": data["gemma_original_vocab"], "new_vocab_size": data["gemma_original_vocab"] + len(clean_tokens)}, open("lao_missing_tokens_clean.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
```

Step 2.3) Load clean missing tokens and add them to Gemma tokenizer.
```python
import json
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

MODEL_ID = "google/gemma-4-E4B"
token_data = json.load(open("lao_missing_tokens_clean.json", "r", encoding="utf-8"))
new_tokens = token_data["tokens"]

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, trust_remote_code=True)
original_vocab_size = len(tokenizer)
num_added = tokenizer.add_tokens(new_tokens)
print(f"Vocab size: {original_vocab_size} -> {len(tokenizer)} (+{num_added})")
```

Step 2.4) Before vs after surgery comparison.
```python
original_tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)

test_texts = [
    "ສະບາຍດີ",
    "ນະຄອນຫຼວງວຽງຈັນ ເປັນນະຄອນຫລວງຂອງປະເທດລາວ",
    "ພາສາລາວມີ 27 ພະຍັນຊະນະ",
    "How can I help you today?",
]
for text in test_texts:
    old_tokens = original_tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    new_tokens_after = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    reduction = ((len(old_tokens) - len(new_tokens_after)) / len(old_tokens)) * 100
    print(text, f"-> {len(old_tokens)} to {len(new_tokens_after)} ({reduction:.1f}% reduction)")
```

Step 2.5) Save surgery model for next CPT step.
```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
import os

OUTPUT_DIR = "./models/gemma4_lao_base_v1"
os.makedirs(OUTPUT_DIR, exist_ok=True)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, trust_remote_code=True)
model.resize_token_embeddings(len(tokenizer))
model.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR, max_shard_size="2GB", safe_serialization=True)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR)
```

Example output:
```bash
Missing Lao tokens to add: 28,022
Gemma original vocab:      262,144
New vocab size:            290,166

BEFORE vs AFTER SURGERY
- ສະບາຍດີ: 4 -> 2 tokens (50.0% reduction)
- ນະຄອນຫຼວງວຽງຈັນ...: 24 -> 4 tokens (83.3% reduction)
- ພາສາລາວມີ 27...: 15 -> 6 tokens (60.0% reduction)
- How can I help you today?: 7 -> 7 tokens (0.0% reduction)

SURGERY SUMMARY
Vocab size: 262,144 -> 290,166 (+28,022)
Saved to: ./models/gemma4_lao_base_v1
```

Actual results from my run: missing Lao tokens = 31,279, cleaned tokens added = 28,022, and Gemma vocab changed from 262,144 to 290,166. Tokenization improved significantly on Lao sentences, while English tokenization stayed unchanged.

sections.title: Step 3 — Continual Pre-Training (CPT)
sections.body:
Step 3 is Continual Pre-Training (CPT) on Lao corpus using the surgery base model from Step 2. In simple terms: Step 2 fixes tokenization, and Step 3 teaches those new Lao tokens with real Lao context so the model can predict Lao text naturally.

Step 3.1) Check GPU and load the surgery base model in 4-bit mode.
```python
import torch
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "No GPU")
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    dtype=torch.float16,
    load_in_4bit=True,
    token=True,
    fix_tokenizer=False,
)
```

Step 3.2) Add QLoRA adapters and train on normalized Lao corpus.
```python
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import TrainingArguments, DataCollatorForLanguageModeling
from trl import SFTTrainer

model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(model, r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0, bias="none", use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth", random_state=42,
    target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj","gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj","embed_tokens","lm_head"])

dataset = load_dataset("text", data_files="lao_merged_corpus_normalized.txt", split="train")
dataset = dataset.filter(lambda x: len(x["text"].strip()) > 10)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=dataset.map(lambda e: {"input_ids": tokenizer(e["text"], truncation=True, max_length=512)["input_ids"], "labels": tokenizer(e["text"], truncation=True, max_length=512)["input_ids"]}),
    dataset_text_field=None,
    data_collator=DataCollatorForLanguageModeling(tokenizer=tokenizer, mlm=False),
    args=TrainingArguments(output_dir="./checkpoints/lao_cpt", num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=1, gradient_accumulation_steps=16, learning_rate=2e-4, fp16=True, optim="adamw_8bit", report_to="none"),
    max_seq_length=512,
)
trainer.train()
```

Step 3.3) Save LoRA + merged checkpoints, then run quick sanity generation.
```python
save_path = "./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1"
model.save_pretrained(save_path + "_lora")
model.save_pretrained_merged(save_path + "_merged", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit")

FastLanguageModel.for_inference(model)
```

Example output (short):
```bash
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090
Total samples after filter: 53,000
Training: 3 epochs | final loss ~0.60
Saved: ./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1_lora
Saved: ./models/gemma4_lao_cpt_v1_merged
```

Result: after CPT, the model is Lao-aware at the language-modeling level and ready for Step 4 supervised fine-tuning.

sections.title: Step 4 — Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
sections.body:
Step 4 is Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): after CPT teaches language structure, SFT teaches assistant behavior (instruction-following, clearer answers, chat alignment).

Pipeline status in my project:
```bash
Step 1: Vocab Surgery -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1
Step 2: CPT          -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-cpt-v1
Step 3: SFT          -> AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Step 4.1) Use CPT output as base and train SFT LoRA on Lao instruction data.
```python
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel

model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    load_in_4bit=True,
    token=True,
)
# then load CPT adapter, merge, and run SFT training on alpaca_lao_sft_3000.jsonl
```

Step 4.2) Save and upload SFT adapter.
```python
# Output adapter repo
# AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Step 4.3) Inference with Gemma chat format.
```python
def ask(question):
    text = f"<start_of_turn>user\n{question}<end_of_turn>\n<start_of_turn>model\n"
    # tokenize + generate
```

Example output (short):
```bash
Dataset: 2,999 samples
Epochs: 3 | Steps: 564
Loss: 0.4978 -> 0.4275 (-16.9%)
Training time: ~49 min on RTX 4090
Cost: ~$0.24
Saved adapter: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1
```

Result: `gemma-4-lao-instruct-v1` becomes instruction-following and ready to merge into a single full model.

sections.title: Step 5 — Merge and Evaluate
sections.body:
Step 5 is Merge and Evaluate: merge CPT + SFT adapters into one standalone model so deployment is simpler (single repo, no adapter stacking at runtime).

Step 5.1) Load base model in full precision (no 4-bit) for safe merge.
```python
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-base-v1",
    max_seq_length=512,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    load_in_4bit=False,
    token=True,
)
```

Step 5.2) Apply and merge CPT adapter, then SFT adapter.
```python
# Merge CPT -> merge_and_unload()
# Merge SFT -> merge_and_unload()
```

Step 5.3) Quick QA sanity test (Lao + English prompts), then save merged model.
```python
model.save_pretrained_merged("./gemma4-lao-full", tokenizer, save_method="merged_16bit")
```

Step 5.4) Upload full model.
```python
# Repo: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full
```

Example output (short):
```bash
CPT merged: ✅
SFT merged: ✅
Saved: ./gemma4-lao-full
Uploaded: AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full
```

Result: one full Lao Gemma model (`AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full`) that can be loaded directly with `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...)`.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
sections.body:
Reflecting on the full build, five engineering lessons stand out:
1. Vocabulary surgery is mandatory for Lao. Without adding missing Lao tokens, token fragmentation is severe and both context efficiency and training quality degrade quickly.
2. Clean data beats big data. A normalized and deduplicated Lao corpus (published as `AOYPSK/lao_text_corpus`) gave far better downstream behavior than noisy web text.
3. Two-stage adaptation works well for low-resource languages: CPT first for language structure, then SFT for assistant behavior.
4. Adapter-based training is cost-effective. QLoRA + staged merging made it practical to iterate quickly on consumer-grade cloud GPUs.
5. Evaluation must be bilingual and domain-specific. The model can stay strong in English while improving Lao fluency, but factual reliability still depends heavily on high-quality Lao instruction data.

sections.title: What's Next
sections.body:
The current public artifacts on Hugging Face are:
- Full model: `AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full`
- Lao corpus dataset: `AOYPSK/lao_text_corpus`

Next priorities are:
1. Expand instruction data with native human-written Lao QA and task-style prompts (reduce hallucination on local topics).
2. Run formal benchmark suites for both fluency and factuality (including Lao-specific and cross-lingual checks).
3. Build an OCR + document understanding pipeline on top of `AOYPSK/gemma-4-lao-full` for real Lao document workflows.
4. Export optimized inference formats (GGUF / quantized variants) for lower-cost deployment on local and edge environments.

title: The Absolute Beginner’s Guide to Flutter: From Zero to First App (iOS & Android)
excerpt: A practical beginner guide to set up Flutter on Windows and macOS, run your first app on iOS and Android, and avoid common environment setup issues.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Flutter is a game-changer for cross-platform development, especially if you come from web or backend systems. But in professional teams, "it runs on my machine" is not good enough. We need a reproducible setup that every engineer (and intern) can bootstrap with minimal friction.
This guide walks through a robust Flutter setup on both Windows and macOS, with the engineering mindset I use in real projects: clean environment boundaries, deterministic tooling, and repeatable verification steps.

Platform support summary:
- macOS: can build for both iOS and Android. Required if you want to ship to the App Store.
- Windows: can build for Android only. iOS builds require a Mac (or a remote macOS build server / CI like Codemagic / GitHub Actions macOS runners).

sections.title: Phase 1 — Environment Philosophy and Prerequisites
sections.body:
Start with a dedicated development directory to avoid permission conflicts and scattered SDK paths.

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
mkdir -p ~/Dev
cd ~/Dev
```

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path C:\Dev
Set-Location C:\Dev
```
Keep the path short and free of spaces (e.g., `C:\Dev`, not `C:\Users\My Name\Documents\Dev`). Long paths and spaces are a common source of obscure Flutter / Gradle errors on Windows.

Core prerequisites (both OS):
1) Visual Studio Code (recommended editor for speed + extension ecosystem).
2) Git (required to clone Flutter SDK and manage channel upgrades cleanly).
3) Android Studio (Android SDK, AVD, command-line tools).
4) JDK 17 (bundled with recent Android Studio; otherwise install separately).

macOS only:
5) Xcode (mandatory for iOS build/signing).
6) Optional but recommended: Homebrew for easier package management.

Windows only:
5) Enable long path support and Developer Mode (Settings → System → For developers → Developer Mode = On). This prevents the classic `path too long` and symlink errors during `flutter doctor` and Gradle builds.
6) Optional: install Chocolatey or winget for easier package management.

sections.title: Phase 2 — Installing the Flutter SDK (Git-Based)
sections.body:
For professional workflows, install Flutter SDK via Git instead of manual ZIP extraction. This gives you easier channel switching (`stable`, `beta`, `master`) and predictable updates.

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
cd ~/Dev
git clone https://github.com/flutter/flutter.git -b stable
```
Add Flutter to PATH (zsh example):
```bash
echo 'export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/Dev/flutter/bin"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
flutter --version
```
If you use bash instead of zsh, append the same line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.bash_profile`.

**Windows (PowerShell):**
```powershell
Set-Location C:\Dev
git clone https://github.com/flutter/flutter.git -b stable
```
Add Flutter to PATH (user-level, no admin needed):
```powershell
$flutterBin = "C:\Dev\flutter\bin"
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(
    "Path",
    [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User") + ";$flutterBin",
    "User"
)
```
Close and reopen PowerShell, then verify:
```powershell
flutter --version
```
If `flutter` is not recognized, log out and back in (or restart) so the new PATH is picked up.

VS Code setup (both OS):
1) Install the `Flutter` extension (Dart is auto-installed).
2) Restart VS Code.
3) Confirm the extension sees the SDK path (Command Palette → `Flutter: Change SDK`).

sections.title: Phase 3a — Android Toolchain Setup (Windows & macOS)
sections.body:
The Android toolchain is identical in concept on both OSes; only the install method differs.

1) Install Android Studio (download from developer.android.com, or `brew install --cask android-studio` on macOS, or `winget install Google.AndroidStudio` on Windows).
2) Launch Android Studio once and finish the initial SDK setup wizard.
3) Open Settings/Preferences → Languages & Frameworks → Android SDK.
4) In the `SDK Tools` tab, enable:
   - `Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)`
   - `Android SDK Build-Tools`
   - `Android SDK Platform-Tools`
   - `Android Emulator`
5) Accept all SDK licenses:
```bash
flutter doctor --android-licenses
```
On Windows, run the same command in PowerShell. Type `y` and Enter for each license prompt.

6) Create an Android Virtual Device (AVD): Android Studio → Device Manager → Create Device → pick a Pixel profile + a recent system image (API 34 or 35 recommended).

Windows-specific note: enable hardware acceleration. On Intel CPUs, install `Intel HAXM` via the SDK Manager. On AMD CPUs or modern Intel, enable `Windows Hypervisor Platform` (Control Panel → Programs → Turn Windows features on or off). Without this, the emulator will be painfully slow or refuse to start.

sections.title: Phase 3b — iOS Toolchain Setup (macOS Only)
sections.body:
iOS development requires macOS. If you are on Windows, skip this phase and use a Mac, a cloud Mac service (MacStadium, MacInCloud), or CI runners (Codemagic, GitHub Actions macOS) for iOS builds.

1) Install Xcode from the Mac App Store (large download, plan for 8–15 GB).
2) Open Xcode once and complete the initial component install.
3) Set the active developer directory and accept the license:
```bash
sudo xcode-select --switch /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
sudo xcodebuild -license accept
```
4) Install the iOS Simulator runtime (Xcode → Settings → Platforms → iOS → Get).
5) Install CocoaPods for iOS plugin dependency resolution:
```bash
sudo gem install cocoapods
pod --version
```
On Apple Silicon Macs, if you hit Ruby/FFI errors, prefer installing CocoaPods via Homebrew instead:
```bash
brew install cocoapods
```
6) Launch the simulator at least once to confirm it boots:
```bash
open -a Simulator
```

sections.title: Phase 4 — The Flutter Doctor Ritual (Verification Gate)
sections.body:
Run diagnostics and treat this as your environment unit test. Same command on both OSes:
```bash
flutter doctor
```

A healthy macOS output should show:
```bash
[✓] Flutter (Channel stable)
[✓] Android toolchain - develop for Android devices
[✓] Xcode - develop for iOS and macOS
[✓] Chrome - develop for the web
[✓] Android Studio
[✓] VS Code
[✓] Connected device
```

A healthy Windows output should show:
```bash
[✓] Flutter (Channel stable, on Microsoft Windows)
[✓] Windows Version (Windows 10/11)
[✓] Android toolchain - develop for Android devices
[✓] Chrome - develop for the web
[✓] Visual Studio - develop Windows apps (optional, only if you target Windows desktop)
[✓] Android Studio
[✓] VS Code
[✓] Connected device
```
Xcode will NOT appear on Windows — that is expected.

If any item has `[!]` or `[✗]`, fix it before creating your project. For verbose diagnostics:
```bash
flutter doctor -v
```
This single habit prevents most onboarding pain.

sections.title: Phase 5 — First Project, Run Commands, and Clean Starter App
Common Setup Errors & Fixes
sections.body:
Use this as a quick diagnostic playbook when your setup breaks.

Windows — quick fixes:
1) Error: `cmdline-tools component is missing`
Action: Android Studio -> SDK Manager -> SDK Tools -> enable `Android SDK Command-line Tools (latest)`, then run:
```bash
flutter doctor --android-licenses
```

2) Error: `Unable to locate Android SDK`
Action: set `ANDROID_HOME`, reopen PowerShell:
```powershell
setx ANDROID_HOME "C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Local\Android\Sdk"
```

3) Error: long path / symlink failures
Action: enable Developer Mode, then run:
```bash
git config --global core.longpaths true
```

4) Issue: Gradle hangs forever
Action: exclude `C:\Dev` and Flutter SDK directory from antivirus real-time scanning.

macOS — quick fixes:
1) Error: `CocoaPods not installed`
Action:
```bash
brew install cocoapods
```

2) Error: `xcrun: invalid active developer path`
Action:
```bash
sudo xcode-select --switch /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer
```

3) Issue: iOS simulator does not boot
Action: Xcode -> Settings -> Platforms -> reinstall iOS runtime.

4) Error: permission denied on shell profile
Action:
```bash
ls -la ~/.zshrc
sudo chown $(whoami) ~/.zshrc
```

sections.title: Pro Tips
sections.body:
1) Hot Reload is your feedback superpower; use it constantly during UI work.
2) On older machines, prefer physical devices over emulators to reduce memory pressure. On Windows especially, USB debugging on a real Android phone is much faster than the AVD.
3) Use `flutter pub add <package>` instead of manually editing `pubspec.yaml`.
4) Install VS Code extensions: `Awesome Flutter Snippets` and `Error Lens`.
5) For production apps, start learning Flavors early (Dev/Staging/Prod) to isolate API configs and signing safely.
6) Pin your Flutter version per project with `flutter --version` output committed to the repo (or use `fvm` for multi-version teams) so every machine — Windows or Mac — builds the same binary.

sections.title: Call to Action
sections.body:
If you are blocked by a setup error, share your `flutter doctor -v` output plus OS (Windows version or macOS version) + IDE version. Most environment failures are deterministic and fixable once diagnostics are visible.
If you want, I can write a follow-up guide on integrating AI features into Flutter using either REST APIs or on-device inference (`tflite_flutter`) with production-safe architecture.
